claims.text: Sit at the preacher bench and set the seat height so the chest and upper arms touch the pad; take the curl bar with an underhand grip.

quotes.text: Adjust the seat height so your upper arms and chest are in contact with the pad. Grip the curl bar with an underhand grip.

claims.text: The top of the pad sits under the armpits with the arms fully straight; the feet stay flat on the floor.

quotes.text: The top of the pad should sit comfortably under your armpits when your arms are fully extended. Keep your feet flat on the ground for added stability.
Make sure your chest and upper arms are against the pad on their respective sides, with your underarms snug over it.

claims.text: A seat set too high makes you hunch over the pad and can stop a full squeeze at the top; either wrong height can shift stress from the biceps onto the shoulder.

quotes.text: Sitting too high up will require you to hunch over the pad, potentially preventing you from reaching a peak contraction at the top of the lift.
Either extreme runs the risk of aggravating your shoulders, as you may be displacing stress from your biceps muscles onto your shoulder joints.

claims.text: Press the backs of the upper arms into the pad while curling, and keep the body still, so momentum can't help.

quotes.text: Drive the backs of your upper arms into the bench pad while you’re contracting your biceps to avoid lifting with momentum.
Keep your body still and your upper arms pressed against the pad.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, using too heavy weights

claims.text: Too heavy a load breaks form, for example the upper arms leaving the pad as the body heaves the weight up, which can put the front delts at risk.

quotes.text: Going too heavy compromises your form — for example, your upper arms leaving the pad while you use too much body English to yank up the weight. That can put your anterior delts at risk.

claims.text: Lower slowly by straightening the elbows; if you can't control the lowering, use a lighter weight.

quotes.text: Slowly straighten your elbows to lower the curl bar to the starting position.
Avoid letting momentum take over. If you feel like you can’t control the descent, use lighter weight.

claims.text: Use a long range: lowering well past 90 degrees of elbow bend is part of the lift; if full straightening feels uncomfortable, turn around a little earlier.

quotes.text: When you don’t extend your elbows down well past 90 degrees, you’re cheating yourself out of the full range of muscle-building potential this lift has to offer.
If fully extending your arms feels uncomfortable, you can avoid that position by reversing the movement earlier. But try to keep the range of motion as long as possible for maximum muscle activation.

claims.text: Keep the wrists straight and the chin tucked; bent wrists add load to them and can cause discomfort.

quotes.text: Keep your wrists straight during the movement. If they’re bent, it can put an unnecessary load on them and lead to discomfort and maybe even injuries.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, not locking your wrists

quotes.text: Tuck your chin. Fully extend your elbows. Maintain a neutral wrist position with your preferred grip.

claims.text: Keep the core and back lightly engaged instead of hanging over the pad.

quotes.text: It’s important to keep your upper body activated, and not just “hang” over the pad.

claims.text: The preacher curl works the biceps and brachialis, with the forearm flexors helping.

quotes.text: It primarily targets your biceps and brachialis, but your forearm flexors will also contribute to the movement.

claims.text: On the preacher bench the load is hardest near the bottom: in one dumbbell study the preacher curl reached up to 80% of maximum biceps activity at the beginning of the lift and was high only over a short range (incline and standing curls reached up to 95% in the final phase), and with a barbell the most torque falls when the elbows are straight.

quotes.text: Dumbbell Preacher Curl elicited high muscle activation only for a short range of elbow joint angle.
one performed with a barbell (BAR; in which greater torque was applied when the elbows were extended and biceps stretched)
The submaximal elbow flexion (concentric) elicited neuro muscular activity up to 95% of the maximum RMS value during the final phase of IDC and DBC and 80% for DPC at the beginning of the movement.

claims.text: In an 8-week trial in young women, the preacher curl grew the lower (distal) part of the elbow flexors more than the incline curl did.

quotes.text: We observed a greater increase in the distal elbow flexor thickness in the preacher biceps curl compared to the incline biceps curl
Sixty-three young women performed the preacher biceps curl (n=30) or the incline biceps curl (n=33) for 8 weeks, twice a week.

claims.text: Across many activities (not preacher curls specifically), a video study found most distal biceps tendon ruptures happened with the palm up and the elbow nearly straight; biceps curls were among the activities.

quotes.text: Mechanisms of injury included deadlift, bicep curls, calisthenics, arm wrestling, heavy lifting, and boxing.
In all, 98% of ruptures occurred with the arm in supination and 89% occurred at 0° to 10° of elbow flexion.

claims.text: Tempo (up = lifting, down = lowering): about 1 s up and a slow 2 s down, inside ACSM's moderate speed of 1-2 s each way, which is stated for advanced training (LR-15). BarBend's "adding that squeeze at the top" gives no pause or seconds, so pause is 0.

quotes.text: at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Slowly straighten your elbows to lower the curl bar to the starting position.

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: The NHS advises people with wrist pain to stop or cut down the activities causing it and not to lift heavy objects or grip anything too tightly (NHS wrist-pain self-care advice, applied here to training; R-LB5-2). The source is data only.

plate.viewWhy: The angled pad, the arm lying on it (c2, c4) and the elbow bend all read side-on; the fault (arms lifting off the pad, c5) is a front-to-back move. Census view is side.
plate.equipment: Preacher bench: seat plus angled arm pad (preacherPad); EZ curl bar (c1). Seat height puts the pad top under the armpits (c2).
plate.start: Seated, feet flat (c2); chest and upper arms on the pad, pad top under the armpits (c1, c2); elbows straight or nearly so, bar in an underhand grip (c1, c7); wrists straight (c8); chin tucked (c8).
plate.end: Elbows bent, bar near the shoulders (c1 grip kept); backs of the upper arms still pressed into the pad (c4); torso still, not hunched (c3, c9); wrists straight (c8).

mistake.what: Upper arms lifting off the pad as the body heaves the bar up.
mistake.why: It comes from a load that is too heavy and can put the front delts at risk.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: the upper arms leaving the pad as the body heaves a heavy bar up (c5). Step 1 set aside: StrengthLog's "Typically, most lifters prefer to stay in the medium to high rep range" is about rep range; "it is often easier to focus on the muscles worked" is about machines; Oliveira's "most lifters may choose a different load" is about a load; Jukes's "the usual arm position during DBTR was forearm supination and elbow extension" (c13) is about tendon ruptures across many activities and names no fault of this exercise; Jukes's "This has been commonly paraphrased as an 'eccentric contracture to a flexed elbow'.", "Both definitions have been frequently used in the literature with little objective analysis or citation." and "the muscle contraction was typically isometric" are about literature wording or a rupture across many activities, and name no fault of this exercise; BarBend's "Below are some of the most common questions" is the FAQ; the 'Common ... Mistakes' headings are headings. Step 2: two candidates are tied to harm: the arms leaving the pad (BarBend: "That can put your anterior delts at risk.", c5) and bent wrists (StrengthLog: "If they’re bent, it can put an unnecessary load on them and lead to discomfort and maybe even injuries.", c8). Both are on a common-mistakes list and each has one harm source, both direct. StrengthLog's list names both, the arms-on-pad fix ("Keep your body still and your upper arms pressed against the pad.") in its first item and the wrists second, so the arms leaving the pad win; BarBend's list (the anchor, written for this exercise) also opens with it. Set aside: the seat height (c3, "Either extreme runs the risk of aggravating your shoulders") is a setup choice, not a candidate (LR-31); "This forward flexed position might cause discomfort for your front delts" is about the exercise's position, not a fault. drawable is true: the side view shows the upper arms lifted off the pad. Pick unchanged; handlingMistakes already has it first. Reading B (verify note 1, LB5): StrengthLog's first item is the too-heavy load, which states the pad cue but not the fault, so no list names both faults; step 3's count is then 2-2 (BarBend and StrengthLog tell the lifter to avoid each, c4, c8), and the first tied fault on the earliest list written for this exercise, BarBend's 'Treating it Like a Strength Exercise', is the pad fault; the pick is the same.

rows.means: Fault: the wrists bent up or down under load.
rows.fix: Stop and don't train through the pain. Keep the wrist straight.
